title: Plastic in the Ocean
description: The scale of ocean plastic pollution and the search for solutions.
instructions: Read the article about plastic pollution in the oceans, then answer the questions. Choose the best answer for each question.

paragraphs.text: Since the mass production of plastic began in the 1950s, the material has transformed almost every aspect of daily life. It is cheap, light and remarkably durable, which explains its popularity in everything from food packaging to clothing. Unfortunately, the same durability that makes plastic so useful also makes it a serious environmental threat, because a single bottle can take hundreds of years to break down.

Scientists estimate that millions of tonnes of plastic enter the world's oceans every year. Much of it is carried there by rivers, particularly in regions where waste collection systems are inadequate or non-existent. Once in the sea, ocean currents can gather the debris into vast floating patches, the best known of which lies in the North Pacific and covers an area several times the size of France.

The consequences for marine life are severe. Sea turtles frequently mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, while seabirds feed fragments of plastic to their chicks. Over time, larger items are broken down by sunlight and waves into microplastics, tiny particles that are almost impossible to remove. These particles have been found in fish, shellfish and even drinking water, raising concerns about their possible effects on human health.

A variety of solutions have been proposed. Some engineers have designed floating barriers that collect rubbish from the surface of the sea, although critics point out that such devices cannot capture the microplastics that sink below. Many governments have introduced bans or taxes on single-use items such as bags and straws, and these measures have led to noticeable reductions in their use. Meanwhile, researchers are developing biodegradable alternatives, though these are often more expensive and do not always break down as easily as advertised.

Most experts agree that cleaning up the oceans, while valuable, is far less effective than preventing plastic from reaching them in the first place. This means improving waste management in developing countries, designing products that can be reused or recycled more easily, and persuading consumers to change their habits. As one marine biologist put it, "When the bath is overflowing, you turn off the tap before you reach for the mop."

Not all ocean plastic comes from land, however. A significant share of the larger debris consists of fishing nets, ropes and other equipment that has been lost or deliberately abandoned at sea. These so-called 'ghost nets' can drift for years, continuing to trap fish, seals and turtles long after anyone has stopped using them. Because they are made to be strong, they are especially difficult to break apart. Some fishing communities now run schemes that pay crews to bring old nets back to port, where the material can be recycled into new products such as carpets or clothing.

Recycling is often presented as the answer, but its limits are becoming clearer. Many types of plastic are difficult or uneconomic to recycle, and only a small proportion of all the plastic ever produced is thought to have been recycled at all. In some cases, waste collected for recycling in wealthier countries has been shipped abroad to places that lack the facilities to process it properly, where some of it may end up being burned or dumped. Critics therefore warn that putting a bottle in the recycling bin can give consumers a comforting sense of having solved the problem, when in reality the bottle's journey may be far less tidy.

Because plastic pollution crosses national borders, many observers believe that international cooperation is essential. Ocean currents carry debris from one country's coastline to another's, so no nation can solve the problem alone. There is also growing pressure on manufacturers to take responsibility for the packaging they produce, for example by designing refillable containers or helping to pay for waste collection. Individual choices still matter, but campaigners argue that it is unfair to expect shoppers alone to fix a problem created by the way products are designed and sold. Real progress, they suggest, will require action from governments, businesses and consumers at the same time.

questions.text: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Plastic is the most useful material ever invented.
Floating barriers have solved the problem of ocean plastic.
Only sea turtles are harmed by plastic pollution.
Ocean plastic is a serious and growing problem, and preventing it is more effective than cleaning it up.
questions.explanation: The article describes the scale and effects of the problem, reviews solutions, and concludes that prevention is most effective.

evidence.quote: makes it a serious environmental threat
is far less effective than preventing plastic from reaching them in the first place

questions.text: According to paragraph 2, how does much of the plastic reach the oceans?
options: It is carried by rivers.
It is dropped from ships.
It is blown from beaches by the wind.
It falls from aeroplanes.
questions.explanation: The text says much of the plastic is carried to the sea by rivers.

evidence.quote: Much of it is carried there by rivers

questions.text: In paragraph 2, the word "inadequate" is closest in meaning to:
options: modern
expensive
not good enough
very large
questions.explanation: Inadequate waste collection systems are ones that are not good enough, which is why plastic reaches rivers.

evidence.quote: where waste collection systems are inadequate or non-existent

questions.text: What are microplastics, according to the article?
options: Plastic bags that look like jellyfish
Tiny particles formed when larger plastic items break down
A new type of biodegradable material
Floating patches of rubbish in the Pacific
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that sunlight and waves break larger items into tiny particles called microplastics.

evidence.quote: larger items are broken down by sunlight and waves into microplastics, tiny particles that are almost impossible to remove

questions.text: What can be inferred about floating barriers?
options: They are the best solution available.
They are too expensive to build.
They only solve part of the problem.
They are harmful to sea turtles.
questions.explanation: They collect surface rubbish but cannot capture microplastics that sink, so they only address part of the problem.

evidence.quote: such devices cannot capture the microplastics that sink below

questions.text: What effect have bans and taxes on single-use items had?
options: They have led to noticeable reductions in their use.
They have had no effect at all.
They have made biodegradable products cheaper.
They have removed microplastics from drinking water.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says these measures have led to noticeable reductions in use.

evidence.quote: these measures have led to noticeable reductions in their use

questions.text: What does the article suggest about biodegradable alternatives?
options: They are cheaper than ordinary plastic.
They have completely replaced plastic bags.
They break down faster than any other material.
They may not be as effective as companies claim.
questions.explanation: The text says they do not always break down as easily as advertised, so claims about them may be exaggerated.

evidence.quote: do not always break down as easily as advertised

options: To describe how to clean a bathroom
To illustrate the idea that stopping plastic at its source should come before cleaning up
To show that cleaning up the oceans is pointless
To introduce a new topic about water shortages

evidence.quote: When the bath is overflowing, you turn off the tap before you reach for the mop.

questions.text: Which statement best reflects the writer's overall argument?
options: Ocean plastic has many sources, and tackling it requires prevention and action at several levels.
Recycling has already solved most of the problem.
Ocean plastic is mainly the fault of the fishing industry.
Consumers alone are responsible for ocean plastic.
questions.explanation: The writer stresses prevention over clean-up and ends by saying that governments, businesses and consumers must all act.

evidence.quote: far less effective than preventing plastic from reaching them in the first place
will require action from governments, businesses and consumers at the same time

To show how the quality that makes plastic useful also makes it harmful
To explain how plastic is manufactured
To suggest that bottles should be kept for many years

evidence.quote: the same durability that makes plastic so useful also makes it a serious environmental threat

transparent
inexpensive
long-lasting
questions.explanation: Durable things last a long time, which is why plastic takes so long to break down.

options: Drinking water is now unsafe everywhere.
Plastic pollution may affect people as well as marine animals.
Microplastics are easy to remove from water.
Fish are the main source of drinking water.
questions.explanation: Their presence in drinking water raises concerns about human health, so the problem is not limited to sea creatures.

evidence.quote: raising concerns about their possible effects on human health
